item.title: Fox News Digital leads in unique visitors, other key metrics against CNN, NY Times during August
item.description: Fox News Digital hit 76 million unique visitors and 1.47 billion multiplatform views in August 2026, leading all competitors per Comscore data.
item.content:encoded:
Fox News Digital closed the summer trouncing other news organizations across key metrics, including in unique visitors.

During the month of August 2026, Fox News Digital reached 76 million unique visitors on desktop and mobile devices, leading the metric for four months straight, according to Comscore. CBS News came in second 70 million unique visitors, followed by NBC News' 65 million, The New York Times' 63 million, CNN's 56 million and ABC News' 29 million.

Fox News Digital maintained its dominance in multiplatform views and multiplatform minutes last month, reaching 1.47 billion and 3.2 billion respectively. The New York Times trailed in second with 1.27 billion multiplatform views and 1 billion multiplatform minutes. CNN trailed even further with 415 million multiplatform views and 647 million multiplatform minutes.

FOX NEWS CHANNEL TOPS NBC, ABC AND CBS IN KEY RATINGS MEASURABLE FOR SECOND STRAIGHT SUMMER

August 2026 marked Fox News Digital's 28th consecutive month as the top news brand in multiplatform views and the 66th consecutive month in multiplatform minutes.

FOX NEWS DIGITAL THUMPS ALL NEWS BRANDS, INCLUDING BROADCAST NETWORKS, IN KEY PERFORMANCE INDICATORS DURING JULY

Fox News also maintained its status as the most engaged news brand across social media for the 144th consecutive month, totaling a whopping 85 million interactions, according to Emplifi and Comscore Social. More than 26 million of those interactions came from Facebook, 14.5 million were on Instagram and 4.7 million came from X.

On TikTok, Fox News notched more than 39 million interactions, a staggering 80% increase from last year.

FOX NEWS SURGES 29% IN UNIQUE VISITORS DURING Q2, WHILE CNN POSTS ITS WEAKEST DIGITAL AUDIENCE SINCE 2015

Collectively, Fox News reached 1.4 billion video views across social media platforms throughout August.

item.title: King Charles responds to Charles Spencer's claims about Princess Diana in a rare statement
item.description: King Charles broke royal protocol with a rare palace statement responding to Charles Spencer's explosive claims in his upcoming memoir "Swan Song."
item.content:encoded:
King Charles responded to claims made about him in Charles Spencer's upcoming book in an unusual move.

The Daily Mail published an excerpt of Spencer's upcoming memoir, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," on Wednesday, Sept. 16, in which the King's former brother-in-law alleged a heated conversation he had with Charles following the death of his sister and the former Princess of Wales, Princess Diana.

"Prince Charles continued his stream of anger, without me interrupting. Then he stopped. I assumed the pause signaled an effort to bring himself under control, but then he unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death," Spencer alleged, according to the Daily Mail. " ‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough!’"

According to the excerpt, the disagreement between King Charles and the 9th Earl of Spencer was regarding the decision to have Prince William and Prince Harry, then 15 and 12, walk behind their mother's casket during the funeral procession.

KING CHARLES CONSIDERED QUEEN CAMILLA 'NON-NEGOTIABLE' AFTER PRINCESS DIANA, AUTHOR CLAIMS

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson issued a rare statement on behalf of the King responding to Spencer's claims.

"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," the statement read, per People.

Princess Diana died in August 1997 at age 36 after suffering injuries sustained following a car accident in the Pont de l'Alma tunnel in Paris, France. Her partner, Dodi Fayed, and the driver, Henri Paul, also died in the crash.

At the time of her death, she and King Charles had been divorced for one year. The two married in July 1981, announced their separation in December 1992 and finalized their divorce in August 1996.

Prince Harry wrote about the decision to have him and his brother walk behind their mother's coffin in his 2023 memoir, "Spare," writing that "several adults were aghast" and that "mummy’s brother, Uncle Charles, raised hell," and that he told the royal family, "You can’t make these boys walk behind their mother’s coffin! It’s barbaric."

This is not the first time Spencer has spoken about his opposition to the boys walking behind their mother's coffin. He told BBC Radio 4’s Today in 2017 that he found the decision "bizarre and cruel."

"It was the most horrifying half an hour of my life," he said. "It was just ghastly. And it was far worse than having to deliver a speech at the end of it. It was the worst part of the day by a considerable margin, walking behind, well, my sister’s body, with two boys who were obviously massively grieving their mother."

"And it was this sort of bizarre circumstance where we told you had to look straight ahead," he continued. "But the feeling, the sort of crashing tidal wave of grief coming at you as you went down this sort of tunnel of deep emotion, it was really harrowing actually and I still have nightmares about it now."

"Swan Song: Diana, My Sister" is set to be released on Tuesday, Sept. 22.

item.title: Chase Briscoe says deer hunting gives him a bigger rush than driving 200 mph in NASCAR
item.description: Chase Briscoe says deer hunting now gives him a bigger adrenaline rush than NASCAR racing, and his 4-year-old son Brooks is already hooked too.
item.content:encoded:
Chase Briscoe has spent years chasing adrenaline at nearly 200 miles per hour. Apparently, that still isn’t enough.

The NASCAR driver says deer hunting now gives him a rush that rivals — and may even surpass — anything he feels behind the wheel.

"It’s the closest thing I’ve ever been able to come to racing, and honestly, I feel like it’s surpassed racing," Briscoe told OutKick OutDoors.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

That might sound like a bold statement coming from a NASCAR driver, but Briscoe says the explanation is actually pretty simple: racing has become normal.

"You know, the racing deal, I do it so often," he said. "We race 38 weekends a year that, truthfully, the adrenaline kind of goes away because you do it all the time.

"Getting to go hunting and getting to feel that adrenaline is like this drug that I can’t get rid of."

Briscoe, who drives the No. 19 Bass Pro Shops Toyota, didn’t grow up as a diehard hunter. His love of the outdoors started instead around his grandfather’s pond back home in Indiana.

"Ever since I was a little kid, I remember we would go over there every Sunday and would just spend time outside, out by the pond fishing," he said.

Watch Chase Briscoe's full interview with OutKick OutDoors here:

As he got older, fishing became a regular part of life with his friends.

"Especially in my high school years, that was all me and my buddies would do," Briscoe said. "We would go find other little farm ponds or go to creeks or wherever and just go fishing."

Hunting came later.

After moving to North Carolina, Briscoe and his family bought roughly 30 acres that happened to be loaded with deer. A few years ago, he finally decided to give hunting a try.

He was hooked almost immediately.

"I went for the first time and just fell in love with it," he said.

Part of the appeal is the rush. But part of it is the exact opposite.

Briscoe and his wife, Marissa, have three children, and the NASCAR calendar doesn’t exactly leave much room for peace and quiet.

"For me, it’s been just an amazing getaway," he said. "Just to kind of be able to get out in the outdoors and start my morning and just watch the sun come up, or just go out there and be by myself."

He added: "We have three kids, and then obviously the chaos of just my career. You don’t get a lot of time just to yourself."

These days, though, Briscoe doesn’t always hunt alone.

His four-year-old son Brooks has caught the bug, too — perhaps even worse than his dad.

"Brooks is ate up with it," Briscoe said.

North Carolina’s deer season had just begun when Briscoe spoke with OutKick OutDoors, and the two had already been discussing their plans.

"Last night we were talking about it," Briscoe said. "I said, ‘Hey, tomorrow deer season starts. I won’t be home, but Monday maybe you can go with me.’ And he was jumping up and down."

Then Briscoe remembered another conversation from about a month and a half earlier.

"We were just driving down the road, and he said, ‘Hey Dad, I want to talk to you about something,’" Briscoe recalled. "I was like, ‘Okay.’ He’s only 4, and he said, ‘I think this year I’m just gonna just shoot bucks this year. No more does.’"

Briscoe laughed.

"I’m like, ‘Okay, buddy. That sounds like a plan.’"

Brooks has reason to be confident.

The very first time he ever went hunting with his dad, he got a buck.

"It was a total, like, one of those Hollywood stories, I guess," Briscoe said. "Literally the first time he ever went out there with me, he got a buck.

"Not that it was — I mean, it was a tiny little four-pointer — but for him, it was his first experience going out there, and he got to do it."

EVA SHOCKEY JOINS 'TOMI LAHREN IS FEARLESS,' DISCUSSES HUNTING AND EATING BEARS: 'NOT MY FAVORITE'

Brooks helped his dad sight in the rifle and pull the trigger. The following season, Briscoe said his son took another step.

"Last year, he got a doe on his own," he said. "Like, actually lined it up. I mean, I helped him, obviously — he’s 4 — but he got it right on the crosshairs and pulled the trigger."

For comparison, Briscoe said it took him about a year and a half to get his first buck.

"He definitely was beating me already."

But for Briscoe, getting his kids into the outdoors isn’t really about who shoots the biggest buck or catches the biggest fish.

It’s about the time spent together.

"There’s so many distractions in today’s world with phones and tablets and TV and just everything else," Briscoe said. "For me to be able to get them outside and just get away from all those distractions. You get to spend one-on-one time and just make a lot of great memories."

Those memories matter to Briscoe because he still carries his own from childhood.

"I remember going fishing with my grandpa, and some of those memories are some of my favorite memories as a kid," he said.

Now he gets to experience that from the other side.

"To be able to be the one that’s taking my son out there and letting him have these amazing memories — he’ll always remember catching a big bass or getting that big buck," Briscoe said. "That’s just one of those core memories that you never forget."

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

Briscoe is still relatively new to hunting compared to lifelong outdoorsmen, but he’s already thinking about what comes next.

"I would love to do an elk hunt," he said. "I’ve been able to do a lot of really cool whitetail hunts. Even last year, I got to go to South Texas — now two years in a row — and I’ve loved that. But I would love to go out west and do an elk hunt or even a mule deer hunt."

The different terrain and challenge appeal to him, particularly the idea of getting close to an elk with a bow.

"Going archery hunting for an elk, I just find that so fascinating," Briscoe said. "I think that would be one of the coolest things to do, is get an elk and get one that close."

The hiking part? Maybe slightly less appealing.

"I don’t know if I would enjoy that part as much," he joked.

Still, Briscoe hopes he gets the chance someday.

And if he does, there’s already an obvious candidate to tag along.

Brooks.

"He would have the energy too, to be hiking and walking around all the time," Briscoe said. "So yeah, if we get to do it one day, maybe he’ll go with me."

item.title: Democrats embraced AI’s growth before Trump came along — now they want to slow it down
item.description: Barack Obama now urges Washington to slow AI development, but in 2016 his White House praised the technology as the cutting edge of innovation.
item.content:encoded:
Some of the Democratic Party’s most prominent voices are pushing for tighter limits on artificial intelligence, including former President Barack Obama, who has joined calls for a slower pace of frontier AI development after years of Democratic leaders touting the technology’s economic and strategic potential.

"We need government – and specifically our leaders in Washington – to get proactive in coming up with concrete proposals, laws and regulations that deal with serious safety concerns, anticipate AI’s impact on jobs and our kids, and make sure that AI’s benefits are widely spread," Obama said in a statement Monday night.

Obama’s latest comments put greater emphasis on slowing frontier AI development than his White House did in 2016, when his administration highlighted the technology’s economic potential while also warning about disruption and calling for policy responses. Democrats have long paired enthusiasm for AI’s economic and strategic potential with warnings about its risks, but some of the party’s most prominent voices are now going further — calling for a slower pace of frontier AI development and tougher limits on how the technology is built and deployed.

Attorney General Todd Blanche argued Tuesday that Democrats’ renewed focus on the potential risks of artificial intelligence should not be treated as "breaking news," suggesting the timing, months before the midterm elections, is politically significant.

AI EXTINCTION WARNINGS DOMINATE HEADLINES AFTER EX-ANTHROPIC EMPLOYEE'S VIRAL POST

"Every Democrat senator suddenly races to a microphone to talk about AI after being eerily silent for months and months, a month. So to talk about the timing of this as being nothing but an effort to influence the midterms, I shouldn't have to say that out loud, of course, that what it is what it is," said Blanche.

The comments came as President Donald Trump has made rapid AI development and the data centers needed to power it a priority, while the administration promotes the technology’s potential economic benefits and faces growing political scrutiny over the cost and impact of expanding data-center infrastructure.

Obama issued a statement Monday on X, writing that AI is "moving at lightning speed – and even faster than those who are engineering it can keep up with."

"Given what we know about technology, we can’t stuff AI back in a box. But we can collectively determine how it's developed and how it’s used, rather than sitting back and letting AI and its fallout happen to us," he wrote. 

He called for regulation, saying, choices to slow down should not be left up to the tech companies.

Any "potential catastrophe will depend on the choices that we make right now," said Obama.

ANTHROPIC CEO CALLS ON AI INDUSTRY TO SLOW DOWN TECH RACE, DRAWING SUPPORT FROM ELON MUSK, SAM ALTMAN

Back in 2016, Obama’s White House touted AI’s potential to open new markets and drive progress across industries while warning about job disruption and broader safety and policy challenges.

"Advances in AI technology hold incredible potential to help the United States stay on the cutting edge of innovation," the White House said in its December 2016 Artificial Intelligence, Automation, and the Economy report.

"Advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology and related fields have opened up new markets and new opportunities for progress in critical areas such as health, education, energy, economic inclusion, social welfare, and the environment … AI should be welcomed for its potential economic benefits," the report added.

Similarly, then-Vice President Kamala Harris said in January 2025 that "it is imperative that the United States remain the global leader on AI" as the Biden administration moved to speed up the buildout needed to support large-scale AI operations.

The Biden administration announced an executive order on Jan. 14 aimed at accelerating AI infrastructure in the U.S., including large data centers and clean-energy projects, as the administration sought to keep the country ahead of its global competitors.

Harris has also recently called for slowing the pace of frontier AI development, arguing that the technology is advancing at an "alarming speed" and urging Congress to establish stronger oversight and safety standards.

"The frontier of artificial intelligence is advancing at an alarming speed. Over the weekend, industry leaders voiced support for an idea that the American people and many AI researchers in their own labs have been calling for: We must responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development," she wrote. 

SEVEN-FIGURE BLITZ AS GOP EMBRACES PUSH TO COMPETE WITH CHINA IN BOOMING NEW TECH SPACE

AI and data centers have quickly become a major midterm issue, as concerns over electricity costs, jobs and the rapid buildout draw increasing attention from candidates in both parties.

President Donald Trump has pushed back on the Democrats’ urgency to caution about using AI, calling the comment a "hoax."

Fox News Digital reached out to Obama, Harris and Schumer's teams for comment.

item.title: Fox News Poll: Squeezed by costs, frustrated voters turn to the Democrats
item.description: Trump's 39% job approval and a 26-point endorsement gap could spell trouble for GOP candidates, a new Fox News survey finds before Election Day.
item.content:encoded:
Roughly three-quarters of voters have rated economic conditions negatively for the past year, and more than three times as many say they are falling behind financially as getting ahead, according to a Fox News survey released Wednesday. And by a wide margin, the Democrats are considered the party that would better handle inflation — at a time when the cost of living and the economy are voters’ top concerns.

FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS

Costs of everyday items are a hardship for voters: 61% say gas prices are a major problem, up from 48% two years ago, while 52% say the same for healthcare costs, up from 44%. Majorities also view housing costs (54%, down from 60%) and grocery prices (62%, down from 66%) as major problems.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS OPPOSE THE IRAN WAR, SEE PROLONGED COMMITMENT

Views on tariffs have grown more negative since last summer, with a high of 64% saying tariffs hurt the U.S. economy, up from 57%. Most Democrats and independents say tariffs hurt, while views among Republicans are mixed (41% help, 36% hurt, 21% no difference).

Overall, nearly two-thirds of voters (63%) say the Trump administration has made the economy worse, including a quarter of Republicans.

All of this contributes to greater pessimism about the future. The portion saying life will be worse for the next generation has risen from 53% two years ago to 62% last year and 68% today, just two points below the high of 70% in 2022.

Only 8% are enthusiastic about how the government is working, with another 23% satisfied. A 68% majority is unhappy, including a high of 33% who are "angry" — driven by 56% of Democrats and 36% of independents vs. just 9% of Republicans.

Despite these economic headwinds and with 48 days until Election Day, maybe the good news for the Republicans is that the Democrats' advantage on the congressional ballot has stayed in the single digits. If the election were today, 51% say they would back the Democratic candidate in their House district and 44% the Republican. The Democrats’ 7-point edge is just outside the survey’s margin of sampling error. Since January, the Democrats have been preferred by 5-7 points.

Women, those under age 35, Hispanic voters, and Whites with a college degree give Democrats their edge, while White men and non-college Whites are strengths for the GOP.

Party loyalty slightly favors the Democrats, as more of them (97%) than Republicans (92%) support their party’s candidate. Independents favor the Democratic candidate 53-31%, with 14% undecided.

Higher engagement boosts Democrats: 64% are extremely interested in the election compared to 53% of Republicans (+11 D margin). And more Democrats (71%) than Republicans (65%) rate their likelihood of voting as a 10 on a 10-point scale, meaning they feel certain they will vote (+6 D margin).

Among those certain to vote (10s), the Democrats’ lead in the generic ballot grows to 11 points (54-43%). 

The edge holds among those in "close" counties, where the 2024 presidential vote between President Trump and former Vice President Harris was within 10 points; the Democratic candidate is favored by 9 points, 52-43%.

"When pundits and analysts talk about the fundamentals favoring the Democrats in this midterm, they are mostly referring to the economy," says Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts the Fox News Poll with Democratic pollster Chris Anderson. "Time is running out for the administration and its supporters to convince voters that things are improving."

Those with a negative view of both the Democratic and the Republican Party ("double haters") favor the Democratic candidate in their district by a 26-point margin.

Voters trust Democrats on most issues in the survey: inflation (by 15 points), large AI data centers (+14), corruption (+11), and foreign policy (+10). The parties are about evenly rated on immigration (R +1).

Prior to this summer, the Republicans held a four-year advantage on immigration, and they led on foreign policy until January of this year. Four years ago, Republicans were preferred by 9 points on inflation.

Democrats have improved their ratings on inflation by 5 points just since July.

Voters trusting Democrats on inflation are more likely to attribute this to Republican failures (51%) than confidence that Democratic policies are likely to reduce prices (47%).

Those views contribute to Trump’s 39% job approval (61% disapprove). His approval has not exceeded 39% since April, when it stood at 42%. His current rating trails former President Biden’s 43% at this point in 2022 and aligns with former President Obama’s 38% before the 2014 midterms. Trump received 43% approval on immigration, 37% on foreign policy (one point above his record low), and 24% on inflation (matching a previous low).

Trump’s standing puts him in a difficult spot to help GOP candidates this year. He lags his party in popularity, holding a 24-point net negative favorability rating (38-62%), unchanged since July.

Sixty percent of voters think the U.S. made the wrong decision in taking military action against Iran, and 77% of that group favor the Democratic candidate in their district.

Four years ago, more voters said a Trump endorsement made them less likely to support a candidate by a 15-point margin. Today, that’s a 26-point gap (25% more likely, 51% less likely).

Still, Trump’s approval matters within the GOP: 52% of Republicans and 75% of MAGA Republicans say it increases their support.

In addition, 53% say the Trump administration is more corrupt than previous administrations compared to 26% who say it is less corrupt.

Both major parties are viewed negatively: the Democratic Party is underwater by 11 points (44% favorable, 55% unfavorable) and the Republican Party by 17 (41-58%).

Nearly two-thirds support raising taxes on the wealthy to expand government programs (65%) and redistribute wealth (63%). However, 52% disagree with increasing taxes on the wealthy so that "nobody gets too rich."

Still, dissatisfaction with capitalism has grown. Fifty-seven percent say the way capitalism works in the U.S. these days doesn’t give people a fair shot, up from 42% in 2019. That shift spans political views, increasing among Democrats (by 17 points), Republicans (+13), and independents (+22).

Poll-pourri

When asked what the most important issue is facing the country unprompted by a list, 34% of voters say the cost of living and 14% say the economy/jobs. The next closest are immigration (8%) and Republicans/Trump/MAGA (7%). Only a handful mention issues like the war with Iran (4%), corruption (4%), healthcare (4%), or AI/data centers (1%).

MAGA holds a 5-point favorability edge compared with the Democratic Socialists of America (35% vs. 30%), although 15% are unable to rate the DSA. Nearly 3 in 10 Democrats view the DSA negatively, and 3 in 10 Republicans view MAGA negatively.

Overall, 59% view labor unions favorably, including 48% of Republicans and 73% of Democrats.

Eighty-one percent of voters favor banning Congress members and their immediate family and staff from trading stocks (up from 75% in January), including 8 in 10 Democrats, Republicans, and independents.

Conducted September 11-14, 2026, under the direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News survey includes interviews with a sample of 1,211 registered voters randomly selected from a national voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (96) and cellphones (821) or completed the survey online after receiving a text (294). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ±3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education, and area variables to ensure the demographics are representative of the registered voter population. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis, and voter file data.

Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.

item.title: US-backed Israel-Morocco deal deepens Abraham Accords amid growing regional threats
item.description: Israel and Morocco will upgrade to full embassies and exchange ambassadors in a major Abraham Accords milestone nearly six years in the making.
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Israel and Morocco agreed Wednesday to upgrade their diplomatic missions to full embassies and exchange ambassadors, nearly six years after Morocco joined the U.S.-brokered normalization drive that reshaped Israel’s relations with parts of the Arab world.

The agreement came during a trilateral meeting in New York between U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz, Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita and Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, one day after officials marked the sixth anniversary of the Abraham Accords.

The original accords were signed by Israel, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain on Sept. 15, 2020. Morocco followed through with a separate U.S.-Morocco-Israel Joint Declaration signed in Rabat on Dec. 22, 2020, restoring official contacts and committing the countries to move toward full diplomatic relations, direct flights and expanded economic cooperation.

IS ISRAEL REALLY ISOLATED? POLLS AND DIPLOMACY POINT IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS

Wednesday's agreement advances several of those commitments. Israel and Morocco agreed to establish full embassies and exchange ambassadors, reinstate direct flights by both Israeli and Moroccan airlines before the end of 2026 and finalize agreements on investment protection and avoidance of double taxation.

The countries also pledged to expand cooperation in trade, finance, technology, tourism, water, agriculture, food security, energy, telecommunications and regional security, according to a Sept. 16 joint statement.

The statement also reaffirmed U.S. and Israeli recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and support for Morocco's autonomy proposal as the basis for resolving the territorial dispute.

But the discussion quickly widened beyond Morocco to whether the normalization framework could eventually include Saudi Arabia.

Asked by Fox News Digital whether Saudi Arabia could be the next country to join the Abraham Accords — amid reports of growing Israeli-Saudi security cooperation against the Iran-backed Houthis — Waltz focused on the regional threat posed by the Houthis and their attacks on international shipping.

"The scourge of terrorism from them is unacceptable to the entire region," Waltz said. "They continue to act as a proxy of the Iranian regime."

NEW RISK FOR US CONSUMERS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS THREATEN A SECOND MAJOR OIL CHOKEPOINT

"You cannot attempt to punish the rest of the world to achieve a political end," he added. "The oceans, trade, and international waterways must remain open."

The comments come as the Houthis have made major gains along Yemen's Red Sea coast near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Reuters reported Sept. 16 that the offensive has exposed new vulnerabilities for Saudi Arabia and strengthened Iran's regional leverage.

The 18-mile-wide Bab el-Mandeb links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and carries roughly 7% of global oil output. Houthi attacks beginning in 2023 forced major shipping companies to reroute vessels around Africa, increasing costs and transit times.

TRUMP SAYS SAUDI NUCLEAR AGREEMENT WON'T MOVE FORWARD WITHOUT ABRAHAM ACCORDS: 'THEY HAVE TO BE A MEMBER'

Sa’ar said the threats at Bab el-Mandeb and the Strait of Hormuz demonstrated why countries with shared interests should cooperate.

"What’s happening in Bab al-Mandab, like what's happened in Strait of Hormuz, demonstrates the significance of all nations that want to respect freedom of navigation, world trade, and cooperate against this kind of modern piracy," Sa’ar said.

He declined to elaborate on any operational cooperation involving Saudi Arabia but made clear Israel wants the normalization framework expanded.

"It is clear that we would like this camp to be widened," Sa’ar told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP CALLS ON ARAB NATIONS TO SIGN ABRAHAM ACCORDS

Bourita, meanwhile, said that Morocco's experience demonstrates that relations with Israel can also give Arab governments practical tools to help Palestinians.

"We can help the Palestinians, humanitarianly, because we have these relations with Israel," Bourita said.

During the Gaza war, Morocco used its ties with Israel to secure a land route for 40 tons of humanitarian assistance into northern Gaza in March 2024. "Is it better to continue in the rhetorics, political positions, while sitting in our cities, our capitals, or take initiatives?" Bourita asked.

"We don't agree with Israel 100%. Each one may have its policy," he said, arguing that Morocco uses the "Abraham Accords spirit" to "promote peace" and "promote stability in the region."

Bourita also pointed to Morocco's participation in Gaza stabilization efforts.

"I think it needs courage to contribute to peace," he said, "and it's easier to keep on making statements and engaging in rhetorics."

Waltz echoed that argument, praising Morocco's humanitarian work and its role in postwar Gaza efforts.

"It is far more than just signing agreements or coming to ceremonies," Waltz said. "The Moroccan government, the Moroccan people are leaning in, in very meaningful ways for a more peaceful future."

item.title: Dermot Mulroney shares 'Young Guns' reunion photo with Emilio Estevez and original cast members
item.description: Dermot Mulroney, Emilio Estevez, Charlie Sheen and Kiefer Sutherland reunited at a Dallas fan event for an epic "Young Guns" reunion selfie.
item.content:encoded:
A number of iconic '80s heartthrobs reunited for a group selfie nearly 40 years after their Western film "Young Guns" was released.

Earlier this week, actor Dermot Mulroney made a joint Instagram post with Emilio Estèvez. Both starred in the 1988 movie. 

"38 years later #youngguns rides again - PALS," the caption of the post read.

NOAH WYLE, MATT DAMON, LEONARDO DICAPRIO STILL CAPTIVATING AUDIENCES WELL INTO THEIR 50S

Also in the selfie was Charlie Sheen, Estèvez's brother; Kiefer Sutherland; Casey Siemaszko; Lou Diamond Phillips; and Terry O'Quinn. The cast of the movie reunited at a fan event in Dallas, Texas, Saturday.

Fans flooded the comment section of the post, praising the men for never aging.

"Does Emilio Estevez ever age? He has the secret to the fountain of youth," one user wrote.

"Emilio looking younger than all of them!" another wrote.

Another Instagram user commented, "If that isn't the most epic reunion I don't know what is!!!!😍"

Mulroney also shared other images from the event on Instagram. 

"When @kiefersutherland says "never had more fun on a movie" #youngguns you know@you had some fun !" the star captioned his post. He also included a nod to the iconic movie with the hashtag, "#didyouseethesizeofthatchicken."

In the images, the men looked like they were having some fun. The final picture in the carousel of images was the cast of "Young Guns" flipping off the camera and smiling.

"Young Guns" is a Western about Billy the Kid (Estèvez) and a group of young outlaws who seek revenge after their mentor is murdered. Their pursuit leads to violence, betrayal and the famous Lincoln County War.

item.title: Hiker in Colorado takes trip to the hospital after being kicked in the back by a moose
item.description: A Westerly, Rhode Island man used a trekking pole to fend off a charging momma moose on a Colorado hike before the animal kicked him in the back.
item.content:encoded:
A man from Westerly, Rhode Island was out on a family hike in Colorado a couple of weeks ago when he, his wife and his son came face-to-face with a momma moose and her baby.

Dean and Rosemary Felicetti were in Colorado visiting their son Gabriel when they decided to go on a hike, reports WJAR. They visited a lake and had their feet in the water before heading back.

As they were making their way down the trail so they could go out for Rosemary's birthday dinner, the couple's son alerted them to the moose ahead.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

"He's like, 'Just don't turn your back. Don't run,'" Dean said. "And so we just started backing up, and a baby moose comes off the switchback towards us."

That's when the family hike became the scariest moment of their lives. Right behind the baby moose was momma moose, and she wasn't there to play around with the family. She charged at them immediately.

BULL BISON SENDS YELLOWSTONE VISITOR FLIPPING THROUGH THE AIR IN CAMPGROUND ATTACK CAUGHT ON VIDEO

Rosemary scrambled up the hillside while Dean and Gabriel tried to fend off the moose. Dean had his trekking pole and Gabriel was throwing rocks and yelling at it.

While Dean tried to poke at the animal with his trekking pole, it reared up and kicked him in the back. The moose then moved on and left the family with minor injuries.

Dean took a trip to the emergency room and had survived the ordeal with only cuts, bruises and a hoof print on his shirt. The couple doesn't blame the moose for kicking their butts.

"We 100% are supportive of the moose's decision as the mom to protect," Dean said. Rosemary added, "She was doing her job."

Who could blame the moose? You're stepping out on its turf and waving around trekking poles. A kick in the back is nothing.

item.title: Media highlights race of Mississippi hanging victim Tasia Fortune but not the race of suspected killer
item.description: Jarques Ratliff was charged in Tasia Fortune's hanging death in Jackson, Mississippi, but multiple outlets initially omitted key facts about him.
item.content:encoded:
The murder of 29-year-old Mississippi woman Tasia Fortune has shocked the nation, and many rushed to claim she was the victim of a hate crime.

The media continue to obscure the facts that dispel the narrative even after the arrest of her suspected killer.

The mother of four was found hanging from a tree outside an abandoned home in Jackson, Mississippi, last month, and her death was described by Democratic Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts as one of several "modern-day lynchings" based on a string of incidents involving Black people being found in a similar manner despite the lack of evidence to support their declaration.

On Friday, 51-year-old Jarques Ratliff, who is also Black, was charged with Fortune's murder. He entered a not guilty plea Monday.

YET ANOTHER DEM RIPPED ONLINE FOR 'INVENTING RACISM' AS LAWMAKERS PEDDLE DEBUNKED ‘LYNCHING’ CLAIMS

Yet the breaking news coverage of Ratliff's arrest put emphasis on Fortune's race but not his.

"Police in Jackson, Mississippi, have arrested a man in the case of Tasia Fortune, the 29-year-old Black woman found hanging from a tree outside an abandoned house last month, following the state medical examiner ruling her death a homicide," CNN began its report Friday and similarly posted on X.

Readers would not know Ratliff's race until they saw his mugshot, which was placed below the sixth paragraph of the story.

In a separate story from Monday about his not guilty plea, CNN again described Fortune as being Black while not giving the same descriptor of her alleged killer — this time burying his mugshot nearly 20 paragraphs deep.

"A man has been arrested in the killing of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman found hanging from a tree in Mississippi last month," NBC News similarly wrote while omitting Ratliff's race.

Notably, neither NBC News' breaking news report of Ratliff's arrest nor its report on his not guilty plea included his mugshot.

ARREST RIPS APART MEDIA NARRATIVE ON DEATH OF BLACK WOMAN FOUND HANGING FROM MISSISSIPPI TREE

ABC News' initial report of Ratliff's arrest failed to even identify his name.

"A man has been arrested and will be charged with homicide in connection with the death of a 29-year-old Black woman whose body was found hanging from a tree in Mississippi last month, police announced Friday," ABC News wrote.

However, the Disney-owned network acknowledged Ratliff's name and race in its follow-up report published Monday.

The Associated Press also scrubbed Ratliff's race from its initial reporting, writing, "Mississippi police have arrested a man in the death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman found hanging from a tree last month."

The AP would later acknowledge his race in Monday's report.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Additionally, USA Today initially refrained from identifying Ratliff's race, beginning its report by telling readers, "A man was arrested Friday, Sept. 11, in connection with the hanging death of a Mississippi Black woman, Jackson police announced," later highlighting how the discovery of her body "was followed by calls for an investigation, including from prominent civil rights attorney Ben Crump." 

Like other outlets, the paper later acknowledged his race on Monday.

A spokesperson for USA Today told Fox News Digital it stands by its initial report, saying it relied on information disclosed by authorities at the time and that its policy is to only publish mugshots "only when the suspect is particularly notable or poses a risk to the community. Ratliff was already apprehended, so neither condition applied."

Representatives for CNN, ABC, NBC and The Associated Press did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

item.title: Popular drugs for bone health linked to significantly lower Alzheimer's risk
item.description: A Hong Kong study of 121,492 older adults links nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates for osteoporosis to a 16% lower Alzheimer's disease risk.
item.content:encoded:
Commonly used osteoporosis drugs were linked to a lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other types of dementia in a large study of older adults.

Among a group of 121,492 adults age 60 or older, the use of nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (NBP) was associated with a 16% lower risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias compared to those who did not take osteoporosis medications.

The risk was 24% less compared to people taking other types of osteoporosis medications.

COMMON CHOLESTEROL DRUG LINKED TO LOWER DEMENTIA RISK WHEN STARTED EARLY

A nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate is a type of medication used to slow bone loss and reduce fracture risk, mainly in people with osteoporosis. Some common types include alendronate, ibandronate, risedronate and zoledronate.

Osteoporosis occurs when the bones become weaker and more likely to break due to a loss of bone mass, according to the National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS). The condition is especially common among older adults.

All adults in the Hong Kong study had recently been diagnosed with osteoporosis or suffered a serious fracture in the spine, humerus, wrist or hip. None had previously taken medication for osteoporosis.

3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS

"Emerging evidence points to a bone-brain axis, suggesting a close link between bone and brain health," study author Ching-Lung Cheung, associate professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at the University of Hong Kong’s Li Ka Shing Faculty of Medicine, told Fox News Digital.

"Our previous studies and those of others have found that people with low bone mass or osteoporosis are more likely to develop dementia later in life. This highlights the importance of maintaining good bone health, which may also help reduce the risk of dementia."

The study, which was published in Alzheimer’s & Dementia, was observational in design.

"Our findings therefore do not prove that bisphosphonate use reduces dementia risk; this needs confirmation in a clinical trial," Cheung said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Generalizability is another consideration, as our study involved only a Chinese population, and it remains uncertain whether the findings apply to other populations."

Another limitation is that baseline cognitive testing was unavailable, which means patients who already developed cognitive impairment may have been less likely to receive osteoporosis treatment.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The researchers also lacked information about the severity of participants’ osteoporosis and bone fractures and their use of over-the-counter calcium and vitamin D.

Other external factors, such as education level, social isolation, air pollution and vision loss, could also have affected dementia risk, they acknowledged.

Although the study findings suggest that older patients receiving NBPs for osteoporosis or fragility fractures had lower rates of Alzheimer’s and related dementias, they do not yet justify prescribing bisphosphonates specifically to prevent or treat the disease.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The authors called for more research that will include wider populations with a focus on whether gender may play a role in the reduced risk.

"The next step is to confirm our observational findings in a clinical trial," Cheung said. "If the benefit is demonstrated, it could have important implications for dementia management.

"We hope these findings encourage patients and healthcare professionals to weigh the overall benefits and risks and use appropriate treatment when indicated."

item.title: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Massie saying Johnson is sending the House home early to prevent Hegseth impeachment

item.content:encoded:
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., filed eight articles of impeachment against Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. 

Under House rules, the House would have to consider Massie’s articles by tomorrow. 

But House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., is sending the House home early today. 

There will be no session tomorrow. That means the House won’t reconvene for business until after the midterms in mid-November. 

Massie contends that Johnson sent everyone home early to avoid a vote related to Hegseth. 

If the House had brought up Massie’s impeachment articles, Republicans would likely have offered "a motion to table." This is an effort to kill Massie’s gambit. 

Thus, the vote would not have been on impeaching Hegseth, but whether or not to set aside Massie’s plan. 

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOUSE CONTROL COULD HINGE ON WHETHER THE OLD POLITICAL RULES STILL APPLY

If the House were to table Massie’s articles of impeachment, the gig is up. It’s done. 

The House never even considered the actual impeachment resolutions. 

But if the motion to table fails, the House then considers the articles of impeachment. 

The motion to table inoculates members from having to take a tough vote on the actual issue. 

REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS MEETS AI AS FEARS OF HUMAN EXTINCTION JOLT CAPITOL HILL

I asked Massie the following: 

Pergram: That would have put them in a tough spot because they would have had to vote on it. Would it have passed?

Massie: "A vote on a motion to table. He may not have survived that vote."

In other words, Massie believes the House could have defeated the motion to table. 

That would have triggered votes on actually impeaching Hegseth. 

And, from Massie’s viewpoint, that’s why Johnson sent the House home.

item.title: Terrell Owens compares Jerry Jones to Donald Trump, says Cowboys owner shows signs of 'narcissism'
item.description: Terrell Owens compared Jerry Jones to Donald Trump on his new podcast, saying the Dallas Cowboys owner will "just say anything" to sell fans hope.
item.content:encoded:
After watching the Dallas Cowboys start off the 2026 NFL season with a loss to the New York Giants, one former "America’s Team" star is taking shots at team owner Jerry Jones.

Pro Football Hall of Fame receiver Terrell Owens, who spent two of his 15 years in the NFL with Dallas, took time on his newly launched "Get To The Point" podcast to speak on the 83-year-old Jones, whom he believes is too worried about headlines and keeping his franchise relevant than actually winning a Super Bowl like he says he wants.

In fact, he invoked President Donald Trump while discussing Jones’ mindset.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"At the end of the day, he’s not worried about wins and losses," Owens said of Jones. "Fans out there, it’s not about wins and losses for him. It’s about the bottom line and the bottom dollar. As long as you guys keep buying Dallas Cowboy merch, he’s raking in dollars. As long as he’s putting a decent product on the field and giving you guys hope that every year is the year, you guys keep buying it.

"He’s just like Donald Trump – he’ll just say anything, and a lot of people are eating it up and think it’s going to be true. Stop it."

Owens continued by saying that Jones is selling Cowboys fans "a fantasy," and even claimed that the longtime owner is showing signs of "narcissism" as he has noted many times he won’t ever relinquish his power atop the Cowboys’ organizational chart.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"Jerry Jones is really selling all these Cowboy fans. He's selling them a fantasy. He's selling them a dream," Owens said. "Jerry, I cannot deny, he is a great salesman. He needs to relinquish some of the control that he has with the team and allow some other people to step in place."

To Owens’ point, Jones has taken the Cowboys to new heights since purchasing the team for $140 million in February 1989. Success quickly followed, as the Cowboys won the Super Bowl in 1993, 1994 and 1996, which restored the team’s previous glory after Dallas won Super Bowl VI (1972) and Super Bowl XII (1978) prior to Jones’ ownership.

But the Cowboys have not made it back to the Super Bowl since that 1996 win, and the supporters of "America’s Team" are desperate to see it happen. Each season, it feels the Cowboys have the chance to do so, but they’ve either fallen short in the playoffs, or worse, missed the postseason entirely.

However, the Cowboys remain one of the most valued teams in all of American sports since Jones purchased the club. According to Sportico, the team is valued at an estimated $15.5 billion if he were to sell it today. Forbes recently valued the franchise higher at $17 billion.

Either way, it’s the most valuable team in the NFL.

item.title: Hawley takes aim at 'corporate welfare' after GOP-backed tax break boosted controversial industry
item.description: Senate Republican Josh Hawley targets opportunity zone tax breaks that tech giants use to build AI data centers, calling the loophole "corporate welfare."
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Anxieties over data centers have cranked up considerably, and one Senate Republican wants to close a tax loophole that he argues tech giants are using as "corporate welfare" to build facilities throughout the country.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., plans on introducing legislation that would tie up a tax loophole for data centers first unleashed by Republicans in 2017 that he charged has been exploited by tech companies to build their sprawling data center facilities. 

It comes as the GOP wrestles with how to handle the data center and AI issue, which has become a major political wedge on the campaign trail, one President Donald Trump has called a "hoax."

'WHY WOULD HE DO THIS TO US?': ONE CRUCIAL TRUMP DECISION IS HURTING HIS BASE, REPUBLICANS WARN

That loophole, Hawley told Fox News Digital in an interview, is for Opportunity Zones, which he said are generally meant for "for low-income areas, low-income housing, low-income businesses or businesses in low-income areas."

"These data centers have figured out a way that they think that they can access all of this money," Hawley said. "So, let's be clear. This is a form of corporate welfare. They don't need any welfare. These people are rich. They can pay their own way."

The tax breaks were first approved by Congress as part of Trump’s first-term tax cuts package, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017. That initial bite at the apple established them as a means to spur investment into lower income or forgotten areas where tracts of land were dubbed Opportunity Zones.

AI'S MASSIVE APPETITE FOR POWER, WATER IGNITES FIGHT IN HIGH-STAKES TEXAS SENATE RACE

They were then made permanent last year through the "big, beautiful bill," and though not explicitly intended to be used for data centers, have since provided a route for tech companies to defer, reduce or outright eliminate corporate gains taxes on their investments in the zones.

Since both tax packages were passed, 8,746 Opportunity Zones have cropped up in the U.S., according to the Department of Housing and Urban Development, just under half of all zones are in rural areas, where tech goliaths have set their sights on building data centers.

And, according to a report from the National Community Reinvestment Coalition, 14% of all data centers are in Opportunity Zones, while just over 17% of all permitted, approved and under construction data center projects are in the zones.

Hawley's forthcoming bill would explicitly exclude data centers from being able to access the tax cuts, adding another barrier at the federal level in an attempt to try and slow their rapid development.

And it comes as Congress scrambles to answer the growing fears over unfettered AI development, which data centers play a key role in.

A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD’S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES

Concerns have rippled through the halls of the Capitol since its return this week after a call from major players in the AI industry to slow development, which came after engineers at Anthropic revealed on X that there was a roughly 10% chance that AI could wipe out humanity within a decade. The topic of reining in the technology is not new.

Three years ago, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., convened several panels with tech CEOs, including one with Tesla CEO Elon Musk and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, to hash out what AI legislation could look like in Congress.

Since then, there has been little to no legislative action taken.

Hawley argued that Congress needs to at least put guardrails on AI and give people the opportunity to sue tech companies if their data and personal information has been used without their consent.

When asked why no real action had happened since Schumer’s series of AI summits, Hawley contended it was "because all the tech CEOs then promptly gave Schumer and the Democrats gobs and gobs money, and they decided that, you know what, maybe this industry is going fine."

"And now what you see the same tech CEOs saying is they want an antitrust exemption so they can all talk together and work together," Hawley said. ‘Any regulations, they want to write them themselves. And they're out there saying, 'The sky is falling, the sky is falling. You need to let us get together, write the regulations and figure out what we're going to do.’ I'm pretty skeptical of that, I have to say."

item.title: ‘Out of control’ killings in Spanberger’s Virginia reach ‘insane’ point as migrant charged in stabbing spree

item.title: Oregon settles with Christian mother denied foster care adoption over gender identity beliefs
item.description: Jessica Bates said Oregon denied her foster care adoption application after she refused to use preferred pronouns or take a child to hormone therapy.
item.content:encoded:
A widowed Oregon mother of five who hoped to give a home to a child in foster care and says she was shut out of the process after telling state officials her Christian beliefs prevented her from affirming a child’s gender transition has reached a settlement with the state allowing her to continue pursuing adoption.

Jessica Bates told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday that she completed Oregon’s foster care training after deciding to pursue adoption but raised what she described as conflicts of conscience with requirements concerning gender identity and the care of children who identify as LGBTQ+.

"In the training, the state wanted me to be willing to put pride flags around the house or if a child should come into my care that didn't identify as binary or whatnot, then I would need to affirm their identity, use their preferred pronouns, support this behavior even if it conflicted with my faith and what I hold to be true," Bates said.

CHRISTIAN LIFEGUARD WHO REFUSED PRIDE FLAG DUTIES AND WAS SUSPENDED IS NOW HEADED TOWARD TRIAL

"When I was on the phone call with them a few months later, they basically kind of set up the litmus test that, ‘OK, well, what if we place a child in your care who wants to transition from one sex to the other, and we want — we need you to take this child to hormone injection appointments. Would you be willing to do that?’" Bates said they asked. 

"And that was kind of the straw that broke the camel's back, because I absolutely would not be willing to do that."

Bates began the process to become certified to adopt in March 2022 from Oregon’s foster care system, but in September 2022 she was denied her application by Oregon due to her religious beliefs, according to Alliance Defending Freedom, which has represented Bates.

ONE OF NATION'S LARGEST CHRISTIAN FOSTER AGENCIES WILL NOT ALLOW LGBTQ COUPLES TO ADOPT CHILDREN

Bates said she told officials that gender affirmation for a child who believes he or she is a different gender than what they were born with is "child abuse," and society has yet to learn the full effects of gender transition hormones.

"It was hard being told you can't adopt or help at all when you know that there were literally like a few thousand kids out there in the foster care system," Bates said. "And just knowing, nope, you can't help, and you're excluded was really hard.

"And, you've probably heard, I am a widow," she added. "My husband was killed in 2017 in a head-on collision. That's kind of a long story in itself, but my five kids and I know what it is to have grief and to lose someone that you love. 

"And just the idea that there's these kids out here, at the same time, while I'm seeing my kids kind of go through life without their dad. And to know there's kids out there that don't have a parent, either want mom or dad that's able to invest in them and love them."

EXCLUSIVE: INDIANA SCHOOL COUNSELOR FIRED FOR SPEAKING OUT ON GENDER IDENTITY POLICY SETTLES LAWSUIT FOR $200K

In March 2023, ADF filed a federal complaint on her behalf, and in December 2023, following a federal district court ruling against Bates, ADF appealed her case to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, asking the court to allow her to access Oregon’s adoption system without discrimination while her lawsuit continues.

In July 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit ruled that Bates can start the process of adopting siblings from foster care without violating her religious beliefs about human sexuality while her lawsuit against state officials progresses.

"This settlement will allow me to continue in the process of looking to foster, to adopt," Bates said. "I plan to do that even though my family life has changed a lot in the last four years. I became a grandmother. My oldest son's married, and he's actually — they're living with me, just because cost of living and everything is so high right now, but I would like to continue the process and this case allows me to do that."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Oregon Department of Human Services for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Reporter's Notebook: House control could hinge on whether the old political rules still apply
item.description: Trump's mid-30s approval and high gas prices favor Democrats, but redistricting and turnout questions could keep House races razor-tight.
item.content:encoded:
Are we playing with the old playbook or a new playbook in the midterm elections this fall?

That’s unclear. It’s hard to determine simply because we’ve seen so much that’s "new" in politics lately.

Norms are cast aside. The American system quaked to its core in recent years. You’ve witnessed an American president win the election by prevailing in the Electoral College but losing the popular vote. To have that happen twice in 16 years (2000 and 2016) is astonishing, considering the fact that such an outcome only unfolded on three occasions before.

You then had a president impeached twice yet return to office a few years later. There was the Capitol riot as arguing continued about the 2020 election.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS WANT MAJOR CHANGE AMID ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL DISCONTENT

If this is the old playbook, Democrats likely light up the scoreboard in November. The party of the president typically loses about 25 seats in a president’s first midterm. Midterm elections are frequently a referendum on the president. That’s why many Republicans are trying to keep President Donald Trump at arm’s length, considering that his polling numbers are anywhere from the mid-30s to 40% on a good day. Gas prices are high. Grocery prices are skyrocketing. The war in Iran lingers. There’s a trade war with one of America’s best allies.

On the old playbook, this portends a disaster for the GOP in this fall’s midterms.

But what if we’re using the new playbook?

President Trump — and sometimes Republicans aligned with him — have shown a remarkable resilience to defy political gravity and norms. Control of the House could come down to just a few seats. What if there are questions about election security and the validity of who won and lost? There’s redistricting. On paper, Republicans probably redrew about five to six seats nationwide in their favor.

If things are tight, we might not know which party wins the House on election night. Perhaps a few days down the road — if not later. That is, unless it’s a Democratic blowout.

And remember what we said a few moments ago about the president’s party losing so many seats in that first midterm? Yes, in a way, this is President Trump’s "first midterm." But not really. He experienced a midterm in 2018. Not that things went in the GOP’s favor that year. There’s no contemporary data on how the party of a president might perform after he’s been out of office and rallied to victory a few years later.

Also, the sheer reduction by both parties of seats which are in play mitigates political "waves" which crash across the political shoreline in House midterm races. Think 1994 and 2010 for Republicans. 2018 for Democrats. Thus, even though many of the factors favor the Democrats, the possibility remains it could be tough for the party to flip the House.

In 2018, the Democrats’ carried an approval rating of 44%. For this time around, it’s 37%. That rivals polling related to the president. In 2018, voters had had enough of President Trump and wanted a change. But because of the polling parity this year, it’s not so obvious that voters are so turned off by President Trump that they automatically gravitate to the Democrats.

Here’s another factor: turnout.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: WHAT’S IN AN ECONOMY?

President Trump has worked hard to tell voters that he’s "on the ballot" this fall. That cuts two ways. President Trump’s presence on the ballot has historically driven people to the polls. In 2016, 60.1% of registered voters showed up. In 2020, an eye-popping 66.4% of all voters cast ballots. And in 2024, 64.3% of those registered to vote did so.

But considering the president’s unpopularity, the cognizance of voters that he’s "on the ballot" could also deter them from turning out. At least those who previously supported him. And those impacts ricochet down to House races. The president’s track record at turning out independent voters in races that count wasn’t great down ballot even as he won the White House in 2024.

Consider that, in the 2018 midterms, 50.1% of registered voters materialized. Just 46.1% voted in the 2022 midterms. It was 36.1% in the 2014 midterms — 41% in the historic 2010 midterms where Republicans won a record 63 House seats.

This "Trump on the ballot" initiative might not resound with voters. Especially since the president conceded — en route to his midterm convention in Dallas — that gas prices wouldn’t decrease until after the election. He also said the U.S. is stuck with the war in Iran through the midterms.

So, how do we know what to anticipate in November?

It’s really hard to read if there’s not a clear wave coming. The best way to postulate control of the House is by going race to race. And that is a painstaking process.

For instance, will Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, D-Mo., have a district in which to run? Missouri Republicans tried to draw Cleaver out of his district earlier this year. Then a court ruled last week that the Show-Me State must use the old congressional districts, likely meaning that Cleaver was safe. Then another judge ruled that voters already cast ballots in primaries. So, the new maps were back, and Cleaver may be out.

All of this less than two months before the election.

MISSOURI HIGH COURT BLOCKS GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAPS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS; TRUMP BLASTS 'RIDICULOUS' RULING

Is there a groundswell for Democrats in Iowa where the Senate seat and governor’s mansion are in jeopardy for Republicans? If that’s the case, Democrats might have a shot of claiming at least two if not three seats there: Republican Iowa Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, Zach Nunn and maybe the seat that Rep. Ashley Hinson is vacating in her quest to become a senator.

How about Ohio? There are competitive gubernatorial and Senate contests. Does a Democratic surge boost Rep. Greg Landsman, D-Ohio? Do the accusations of spousal and child abuse bounce embattled Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio., in what is otherwise a relatively safe Republican seat? 

Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, clung to her seat by fewer than 1,000 votes two years ago. But that was when President Trump carried the Buckeye State by 11 points and Kaptur’s district. Redistricting actually turned Kaptur’s turf slightly more in her favor. But the 80-year-old Kaptur was in a car wreck in August, inhibiting her ability to campaign. Is that a factor?

How well do Democrats perform in Virginia? Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Va., faces former Rep. Elaine Luria, D-Va., who she vanquished in 2022. Could former Rep. Tom Perriello, D-Va., who won in a 2008 upset in a differently-drawn district and promptly lost in 2010, unseat Rep. John McGuire, R-Va.?

Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, is retiring. Former Republican Maine Gov. Paul LePage is running for Golden’s seat. Does LePage benefit from Democratic chaos in the effort to unseat Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine? After all, President Trump won one of Maine’s three electoral votes in 2024, capturing that congressional district over former Vice President Kamala Harris.

We could bounce around the map, district to district, all day like this. But sans a wave, that’s what you must do to properly filet the House races.

Most conventional arrows point in the direction of Democrats winning the House this fall. Yet it probably shouldn’t be this close.

That’s why you have to go by the playbook.

The only question is if this is the old playbook or new playbook?
